LESSON 8 OF 12·CSRF, SSRF & Production Hardening

CSRF, SameSite Cookies & State-Changing Requests

See how Cross-Site Request Forgery abuses ambient browser cookies and how CSRF tokens, SameSite attributes, and method discipline stop it.

Beginner22 min
Why this matters

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks a victim’s browser into sending an unintended state-changing request—such as changing an email address, transferring funds, or rotating an API key—to a site where the victim is currently signed in. Because browsers automatically attach session cookies to cross-site requests unless restricted, the server may treat the forged request as a genuine action by the user.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A user signs into a web application and receives a session cookie stored by their browser.
  • While that session is active, the user visits another page or opens an email containing a hidden form or script that submits a request to the target application.
  • If the session cookie lacks SameSite protection and the endpoint requires no unpredictable request token, the browser sends the cookie and the server executes the action.
  • An anti-CSRF token (or custom header verified on the server) works because a cross-origin page cannot read the token from the target origin due to the Same-Origin Policy.

The background

Historically widespread across form-based web apps, CSRF prompted browser vendors to change the default cookie behavior to SameSite=Lax, dramatically reducing accidental exposure while keeping explicit anti-CSRF tokens essential for sensitive endpoints.

Real-world examples

  • Applications that perform state changes on GET requests (such as /account/delete?confirm=1) remain vulnerable even with SameSite=Lax cookies because top-level link navigations still send Lax cookies.
  • Login CSRF can bind a victim’s browser to an attacker-controlled account so the victim inadvertently saves sensitive data into the attacker’s profile.

What to look for

  • Verify that GET and HEAD requests are strictly read-only and never mutate server state.
  • Check whether state-changing POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE endpoints validate a cryptographic anti-CSRF token or require a non-simple custom header with strict CORS.
  • Inspect Set-Cookie headers to confirm SameSite=Lax or SameSite=Strict is explicitly set.

Open PortSwigger Web Security Academy resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Require unpredictable, session-bound anti-CSRF tokens on all state-changing form and API requests.
  • Never perform state-changing operations on GET requests.
  • Explicitly set SameSite=Lax (or SameSite=Strict for high-sensitivity sessions) along with Secure and HttpOnly on session cookies.
  • Verify the Origin or Referer header on sensitive state-changing requests as an additional defense-in-depth check.
